simple.author: Robert Browning
simple.meaning: A simple choice can be more effective than adding many things.
simple.example: We choose two useful decorations and leave the rest of the table clear.
simple.note: This is a short excerpt from a poem. In the poem, a painter considers artistic ambition; the line is not a rule that less is always better.
simple.answer: The example removes unnecessary additions so that the useful choices stand out.

beauty.text: A thing of beauty is a joy for ever:
beauty.author: John Keats
beauty.meaning: Something beautiful can continue to give pleasure after the first moment.
synonyms: A beautiful experience can stay with us
beauty.example: Long after our walk, I still remember the light on the trees.
beauty.note: The colon is retained from the opening line. For ever is an older two-word spelling of forever. This is a poetic claim, not a measurable promise.
beauty.answer: The memory of the beautiful light continues to give pleasure after the walk.

reading.text: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
reading.author: Francis Bacon
reading.meaning: Reading builds knowledge, discussion develops readiness, and writing encourages precision.
synonyms: Read to learn, discuss to respond, and write to be precise
Different forms of study develop different abilities
reading.example: We read the passage, discuss an interpretation, and write a precise summary.
reading.note: Maketh means makes; conference here means discussion. The historical use of man is retained in the quotation. These claims describe an educational ideal.
reading.answer: Reading, discussion and writing contribute different, complementary skills.

brief.text: brevity is the soul of wit
brief.author: William Shakespeare
brief.meaning: Expressing an idea briefly can make it more effective or clever.
brief.example: Instead of repeating the explanation, I give one clear sentence and wait for a reply.
brief.note: This is an excerpt from a speech by Polonius. His lengthy speech creates irony, so the dramatic context matters. The date refers to the First Folio publication.
brief.answer: The example removes repetition while keeping the important idea.

music.text: If music be the food of love, play on;
music.author: William Shakespeare
music.work: Twelfth Night, Act I, Scene 1 (First Folio)
music.meaning: The speaker imagines music as something that feeds or sustains a feeling of love.
synonyms: Sound is compared to emotional nourishment
music.example: The melody changes the mood in the room, and we listen to the next phrase.
music.note: Orsino speaks this line. Be is an older subjunctive form here. Food of love is a metaphor, and the speech goes on to complicate the speaker’s desire.
music.answer: Food nourishes a body; in the metaphor, music nourishes an emotion.

nature.text: We need the tonic of wildness
nature.author: Henry David Thoreau
nature.meaning: Time in untamed nature can refresh people who spend much of life within familiar routines.
nature.example: After a day indoors, we spend a quiet hour beside the trees.
nature.note: This is an excerpt. Tonic means something that refreshes or restores, not a literal drink. The passage contrasts familiar village life with the surrounding wild landscape.
nature.answer: The example uses time outdoors as a restorative change from an indoor routine.

laughter.text: There is nothing in the world so irresistibly contagious as laughter and good-humour.
laughter.author: Charles Dickens
laughter.meaning: A cheerful mood can spread from one person to others.
synonyms: Laughter can spread through a group
Good spirits can influence the people nearby
laughter.example: One guest starts laughing at a gentle joke, and soon the whole table is smiling.
laughter.note: Contagious is figurative here: it describes an emotion spreading, rather than an infection. The original spelling good-humour is retained.
laughter.answer: The example shows one person’s cheerful reaction affecting the rest of the group.

christmas.text: I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year.
christmas.author: Charles Dickens
christmas.meaning: The speaker promises to carry the spirit of a celebration into ordinary life.
synonyms: Keep practicing generosity beyond the holiday
Let an occasion influence everyday conduct
christmas.example: After the gathering, we continue checking whether our neighbor needs help.
christmas.note: Scrooge speaks this line after confronting the consequences of his conduct. The quotation expresses his resolution; it is not a statement that everyone celebrates the holiday.
christmas.answer: Continuing to help after the occasion turns a seasonal promise into an everyday action.

halloween.text:
Double, double toil and trouble;
Fire burn, and cauldron bubble.
halloween.author: William Shakespeare
halloween.meaning: The repeated sounds create the atmosphere of a fictional spell.
synonyms: A rhythmic chant builds a supernatural mood
Repeated words create a dramatic incantation
halloween.example: At the costume gathering, we read the lines as a piece of theater rather than a real instruction.
halloween.note: The witches chant these lines in the play. Toil means hard work; cauldron means a large pot. The date refers to publication, not to a recorded spoken event.
halloween.answer: Repetition, rhythm and the bubbling-pot image create the fictional atmosphere.
